enrichment.short_title: Mobile termination charge caps upheld against MNOs
key_facts: Oftel referred mobile network operators' wholesale call termination charges to the Competition Commission after proposing price controls.
The Commission found termination charges were well above a fair charge and recommended licence modifications capping charges from 2003 to 2006.
T-Mobile, Vodafone and Orange challenged the Commission's report and the Director's licence modifications, including transitional regulation after new EU telecoms directives took effect.
The dispute centred on whether termination revenue subsidised customer acquisition and whether fixed-network users bore excessive costs.
Moses J dismissed all judicial review claims but granted permission to appeal on the main regulatory and fair-charge issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent consolidated judicial review in the Administrative Court challenging Competition Commission recommendations and Oftel licence modifications on mobile call termination charges.
enrichment.outcome: All judicial review applications dismissed; permission to appeal granted on grounds including SMP regulation, transitional EU regime, fair-charge methodology and targeting of price caps.
enrichment.ratio: The Director and Competition Commission lawfully may regulate mobile call termination charges during the transitional period before full implementation of the 2002 EU telecoms directives, and their calculation of a fair charge and recommended price caps was a reasoned exercise of regulatory judgment not vitiated by irrationality or breach of section 3 of the Telecommunications Act 1984.
legal_issues: Whether price controls could be imposed without a prior SMP designation under the Licensing and Interconnection Directives
Lawfulness of transitional termination charge regulation between April 2002 and July 2003
Whether the Commission's fair-charge model and externality surcharge were irrational
Interpretation of section 3(1) duties of fairness and financeability in telecoms regulation
Whether the Director's continuation notice was compatible with the new Framework Directive

enrichment.short_title: Five-year delay fatal to murder appeal renewal
key_facts: Nur was convicted of murder in May 1996 after a two-month trial based largely on identification and associated evidence.
Single judge leave to appeal was refused in March 1997; the applicant claimed he renewed within 14 days but no Form SJ reached the Criminal Appeals Office.
No renewal or witness forms were lodged for about five years until a fresh Form NG was received in April 2002.
Parts of the summing-up transcript were missing, but the court reviewed available material and the earlier single judge decision.
The proposed appeal raised numerous grounds including Turnbull directions, alibi fairness and violent disorder count addition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) for extension of time to apply for leave to appeal against conviction, with renewed grounds after prolonged delay.
enrichment.outcome: Application for extension of time refused; leave to appeal against conviction not granted.
enrichment.ratio: A delay of nearly five years in renewing an application for leave to appeal, without cogent explanation and where the merits of the proposed appeal are not compelling, is fatal; even assuming a prison-lodged renewal never reached the court, subsequent inaction and the weakness of the grounds justify refusal.
legal_issues: Whether an extension of time should be granted for a very late leave application
Effect of failure to serve Form SJ within 14 days under Criminal Appeal Rules rule 12
Merits of alleged Turnbull and summing-up defects in a joint enterprise murder case
Whether fresh evidence could be pursued without Form W

confidence.notes: Complete single-judge decision with clear refusal on delay and merits.

enrichment.short_title: Coroner system neglect verdict quashed on evidence
key_facts: Scott Robbins hanged himself in a Croydon police cell in September 2000 after arrest for bicycle theft.
Custody records noted dyslexia and a self-harm incident five years earlier; forensic medical examiners found no special suicide precautions necessary.
An inquest jury returned suicide contributed to by system neglect.
The Metropolitan Police sought judicial review to quash the neglect finding, supported by individual officers; the family opposed.
Evidence did not establish a real and immediate suicide risk or gross systemic failure causally linked to death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of a coroner's ruling permitting a neglect/system neglect verdict and of the jury's inquest conclusion after a custody suicide.
enrichment.outcome: Claim granted in part: verdict quashed to the extent it included 'contributed to by system neglect'; no fresh inquest ordered; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: On the evidence, there was insufficient basis to leave neglect or system neglect to the jury under the Jamieson test; a prior self-harm report and lack of officer training did not establish gross failure or clear causal connection where medical assessments found no continuing risk.
legal_issues: When a coroner may leave neglect or system neglect to an inquest jury
Application of R v HM Coroner ex parte Jamieson principles to custody suicides
Relationship between Middleton system neglect and Article 2 after the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether lack of police self-harm training could amount to gross system neglect
Appropriate remedy where a verdict was not properly open to the jury

enrichment.short_title: Scottish lifer transfer does not breach Article 7
key_facts: McFetrich pleaded guilty to murder in Scotland in 1995 and was sentenced to life imprisonment.
He transferred to an English prison under section 26 of the Criminal Justice Act 1961 in September 1997.
Scottish judicial recommendations suggested an eight-year tariff; the Lord Chief Justice suggested 10–11 years; the Secretary of State set 12 years.
No formal Scottish tariff had been fixed before transfer because the Scottish Preliminary Review Committee process had not reached his case.
He argued that the higher English tariff violated Article 7 by imposing a heavier penalty than applicable at the time of the offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's original and subsequent decisions fixing and maintaining a 12-year tariff after transfer from Scotland to England.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no breach of Article 7 found.
enrichment.ratio: Article 7 is concerned with the penalty itself, which for murder is mandatory life imprisonment, not the tariff-setting machinery; section 26(4) requires a transferred prisoner to be treated as if sentenced in the receiving jurisdiction, so fixing an English tariff after transfer does not impose a heavier penalty than was applicable when the offence was committed.
legal_issues: Construction of section 26(4) Criminal Justice Act 1961 after inter-jurisdictional transfer
Whether tariff constitutes a penalty for Article 7 purposes
Difference between Scottish PRC procedure and English tariff setting
Whether Anderson supports equating tariff with penalty under Article 7
Lawfulness of maintaining a 12-year tariff on review

enrichment.short_title: No Article 6 oral hearing for s69 leave
key_facts: BLCT sought leave to appeal an arbitration award on market rent in a Sainsbury superstore lease rent review.
The arbitrator declined to rentalise a £3 million premium paid in a comparable ASDA transaction.
Pumfrey J refused section 69 leave on paper and declined an oral reconsideration under CPR 52.3(4).
BLCT applied to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal that procedural decision.
The dispute turned on treatment of premiums/key money in open market rent valuation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for permission to appeal against refusal of leave to appeal an arbitral award and refusal of an oral hearing on the leave application.
enrichment.ratio: Section 69(5) permits determination of leave applications on paper unless a hearing is required; parties who choose arbitration accept limited court intervention and Article 6 does not generally require an oral hearing for a pure question-of-law leave application where the arbitrator has already conducted a fair private hearing, and CPR 52.3(4) does not apply to section 69 decisions.

Whether Article 6 requires an oral hearing for section 69(5) leave applications
Scope of the Court of Appeal's residual jurisdiction after North Range Shipping v Seatrans
Whether section 69(6) is incompatible with Article 6
Correct treatment of lease premiums in market rent arbitration

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence limitation accrued at service expiry
key_facts: Polley instructed solicitors to pursue a workplace injury claim against Hydro Polymers; proceedings were issued in May 1993 near limitation expiry.
The solicitors failed to serve within four months and obtained an ex parte extension without evidence, later set aside in April 1994.
On 20 April 1994 the solicitors advised Polley to seek independent legal advice about a possible claim against them.
Polley issued proceedings against his former solicitors on 14 April 2000.
A preliminary limitation issue was tried; the judge held the claim time-barred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court preliminary issue trial determining whether a solicitor negligence claim was statute-barred.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; claim held time-barred.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant's underlying action was doomed to fail because there was no good reason for failure to serve within the four-month period, damage accrued when the limitation on service expired, not when the extension was later set aside; a claimant cannot avoid limitation by pleading only later-occurring loss.
legal_issues: When damage accrues in solicitor negligence claims affecting underlying litigation
Application of Khan v Falvey and Hatton v Chafes to service/extension failures
Whether loss arose on expiry of service time or on setting aside the extension order
Whether an ex parte extension without evidence was bound to be set aside on the facts

enrichment.short_title: Larsen trap licence lawful but decoy suffering offence
key_facts: Norman Shinton used a Larsen trap with a live magpie decoy at his home to protect songbirds.
RSPCA informations alleged unlawful confinement under section 8 WCA 1981 and unnecessary suffering under the Protection of Animals Act 1911.
Use fell within a general licence permitting Larsen traps for wild bird conservation where section 8 would otherwise apply.
The decoy magpie was kept for weeks without rotation; veterinary evidence showed poor condition, feather damage and injury consistent with prolonged confinement.
The magistrates acquitted on both counts; RSPCA appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated to the High Court on questions of law following acquittal in the magistrates' court.
enrichment.outcome: Acquittal on Wildlife and Countryside Act charge upheld; acquittal on Protection of Animals Act charge held wrong in law, but case not remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Honest use of a Larsen trap for the licensed purpose of conserving wild birds can suffice under section 16 WCA 1981, but lawful licensed trapping does not preclude a separate offence of causing unnecessary suffering to the decoy bird under the Protection of Animals Act 1911 where veterinary evidence shows substantial unnecessary suffering.
legal_issues: Whether Larsen trap use must in fact promote conservation or only be for that purpose honestly held
Whether compliance with the general licence excludes liability for decoy bird suffering
Whether failure to rotate decoy birds can constitute unnecessary suffering
Interaction of Wildlife and Countryside Act licensing and Protection of Animals Act 1911

enrichment.short_title: Vanished caravan not priority need if already homeless

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Scott Higgs lived unlawfully in a caravan on council land in Hove Park from late 2001.
Council enforcement required removal; before the hearing his caravan disappeared without trace on 30 March 2002.
The authority accepted homelessness and no intentional homelessness but denied priority need under section 189(1)(d).
Higgs argued the disappearance was an emergency disaster akin to flood or fire.
The court held he was already homeless under section 175(2)(b) because he had no lawful place to station the caravan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court appeal against a local authority review decision on priority need for homelessness assistance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no priority need established.
enrichment.ratio: Although the sudden unexplained loss of a caravan may constitute an emergency disaster of a similar nature to flood or fire, section 189(1)(d) requires homelessness to result from that emergency; a person already homeless because he had no permitted place for his caravan cannot show priority need arising from the later disappearance.
legal_issues: Whether unexplained removal of a caravan is an 'emergency such as flood, fire or other disaster'
Construction of section 189(1)(d) after R v Bristol City Council ex p Bradic
Whether priority need requires physical damage to accommodation
Causation where section 175(2)(b) already deemed the applicant homeless

enrichment.short_title: Expanding refused JR grounds at substantive hearing
key_facts: Smith was recalled to prison after testing positive for class A drugs while on extended licence following rape and threats to kill convictions.
He challenged the Parole Board's refusal decision without an oral hearing, relying on Articles 5 and 6.
Silber J granted permission only on Article 6/common law oral hearing grounds and refused Article 5 permission after a contested oral permission hearing.
At the substantive hearing Goldring J declined to reopen Article 5 relying on Opoku guidance.
The Court of Appeal held the judge had wider discretion and that Article 5 and 6 points should be heard together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on procedure where a judge granted partial permission for judicial review after an oral permission hearing and the claimant sought to rely at trial on refused grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; unrestricted permission to apply for judicial review granted; case retained by Court of Appeal for final hearing on Articles 5 and 6.
enrichment.ratio: After a contested oral permission hearing, a judge conducting the substantive judicial review retains a broad discretion to permit argument on grounds previously refused where justice requires; Opoku's paragraph 16 limitations are not exhaustive, and closely related Article 5 and Article 6 grounds should ordinarily be heard together.

enrichment.short_title: Youth burglary conviction quashed over recklessness language
key_facts: An 11-year-old appellant and three older co-defendants were involved in disorder at a Tower Hamlets concierge office in July 2002.
Youth court justices found no case to answer on a joint criminal damage charge but convicted all four of burglary with intent to damage.
Police saw the group near fixed equipment and attempting removal; the appellant said he was looking for his brother.
The written case stated findings of intent to remove equipment and to cause criminal damage on entry.
Oral announcements referred to recklessness and 'a degree of recklessness', creating ambiguity about the mental element applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from the Thames Youth Court against conviction for burglary with intent to cause unlawful damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; burglary conviction quashed; no remittal to a fresh bench.
enrichment.ratio: Section 9(1)(a) burglary requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of intent to commit the ulterior offence at the time of entry; although the case stated may record adequate findings of intent, oral reasons referring to recklessness without clear intention language may give a young defendant the impression the wrong mental element test was applied, warranting quashing the conviction.
legal_issues: Mental element for section 9(1)(a) burglary with intent to cause criminal damage
Whether justices' oral references to recklessness showed the wrong test was applied
Consistency between no-case-to-answer on criminal damage and burglary conviction
Need for clear comprehensible findings when trying children in youth court
